splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means 'and' or 'or,' directly affecting whether defendants with certain criminal histories can avoid mandatory minimum sentences. The split leads to defendants with identical criminal histories receiving dramatically different sentences depending on where they are prosecuted.

positions.label: Conjunctive ('and' means 'and')
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1).

positions.label: Disjunctive ('and' means 'or')
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the rule of lenity should prevail over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous criminal provisions. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit has held that agency deference trumps lenity. The issue is significant because it determines whether ambiguous sentencing enhancements are construed in favor of or against defendants.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over Auer/Kisor or Chevron deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions, meaning ambiguity must be resolved in the defendant's favor.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing the government's anti-defendant reading of ambiguous sentencing provisions to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the Guidelines under Stinson and Kisor.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is entitled to controlling deference or impermissibly expands the guideline text. This split affects the sentencing of many defendants with prior drug conspiracy convictions.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and controlling
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and that inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that the commentary impermissibly adds to the guideline rather than interpreting it, so conspiracy does not qualify as a controlled substance offense.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) when the state law covers substances not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to be federally controlled. Some circuits hold that any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling, while others require the substance to be federally controlled. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-law offenses qualify regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses even if the substance is not federally controlled, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under federal law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) authorizing such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether non-retroactive changes in law can support compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes, alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons. Others allow courts to consider them. The Seventh Circuit in United States v. Black held the Commission's 2024 policy statement attempting to authorize this exceeds its statutory authority, deepening the split.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, and/or that the Sentencing Commission exceeded its authority in U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release, particularly when combined with other factors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly impose punishment for the violation of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts revoking supervised release may punish the defendant for the underlying violation conduct or only for the breach of the court's trust. The Sixth Circuit allows courts to expressly punish for violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split, while other circuits limit the purpose of revocation sentencing to addressing the breach of trust.

positions.label: May punish for violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions, not just for the breach of trust.

positions.label: Revocation addresses breach of trust only
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of revocation sentencing is to sanction the breach of the court's trust inherent in violating supervised release conditions, not to punish the underlying conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 is available to challenge conditions or circumstances of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement), and whether habeas is the exclusive remedy for claims that affect the duration of confinement.
splits.description: A longstanding and unresolved circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is available (or exclusive) for challenges to conditions of confinement, as opposed to the fact or duration of imprisonment. The Supreme Court flagged but did not resolve this question in Preiser v. Rodriguez, and the circuits have developed irreconcilable approaches. The issue arises frequently in challenges to BOP decisions regarding First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus under § 2241 is available to challenge conditions of confinement, including BOP decisions about placement and credit calculations, not just the fact or duration of confinement.

positions.label: Habeas limited to fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is available only to challenge the fact or duration of confinement; challenges to conditions of confinement must proceed through civil rights statutes like § 1983 or Bivens.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to appeals from orders on Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter (subject to a 30-day appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (subject to a 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the motion is civil in nature and ancillary to the criminal case, but a minority of circuits apply the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case and is governed by the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held it belongs to the estate based on the broad scope of § 541(a), while other circuits have concluded it belongs to the debtor. This split directly affects whether Chapter 7 trustees can sell appreciated assets of good-faith converting debtors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor upon good-faith conversion, consistent with the statute's structure, policies, and legislative history designed to protect converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: This case addressed a fundamental rule about withdrawal liability calculations for multiemployer pension plans. The timing of when actuarial assumptions can be selected controls how much withdrawing employers must pay, affecting billions of dollars in potential obligations. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuarial assumptions need not be fixed by the statutory measurement date and may be selected by the plan actuary afterward.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be determined as of the statutory measurement date — the end of the prior plan year — providing greater predictability for withdrawing employers.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervisory period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing calculations for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory authority for judicially-created fugitive tolling of supervised release, and the term runs regardless of absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face Section 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar — which prevents relitigating previously presented claims — in addition to Section 2255(h)'s separate gatekeeping requirements. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any claim they previously presented. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the bar on relitigating previously presented claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing a categorical bar in addition to § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures like ballot-receipt deadlines. The outcome affects the ability to challenge mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election based on competitive injury from allegedly unlawful vote-counting procedures.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate does not have Article III standing to challenge state election rules pre-election, as the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine of 28 U.S.C. § 1291.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether orders denying motions to seal medical records satisfy the collateral order doctrine's 'effectively unreviewable' requirement. The D.C. Circuit held that medical privacy is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appeal, while other circuits have been more restrictive in applying the collateral order doctrine to sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal medical information are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be irreparably lost if review is delayed.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine because the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated through other means, such as protective orders or post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
